html:
The non-cooperation movement of 1920 to 1922 was the first campaign Gandhi led across all India. It turned the Indian National Congress from a club of lawyers into a mass movement.

Two things lit it. One was the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919. The other was the Khilafat cause: Indian Muslims were angry at the Allies' treatment of the Ottoman sultan, the caliph of Islam, after the war. Gandhi joined the two, and for once Hindus and Muslims marched together.

His argument was that British rule rested on Indian cooperation and would fall if that were withdrawn. People were asked to:

  • give back titles and honours;
  • leave government schools, courts and councils;
  • boycott foreign cloth and spin and wear khadi, hand-made cloth;
  • in a last stage, refuse to pay taxes.

He promised self-rule within a year. Students left colleges, lawyers such as Motilal Nehru gave up their practice, and bonfires of foreign cloth burnt in every town. About 30,000 people were in jail by the end of 1921.

On 4 February 1922 a crowd at Chauri Chaura in the United Provinces set fire to a police station and killed 22 policemen. Gandhi, to the dismay of his colleagues, called the whole movement off. He was jailed for six years and served two.
sum: The non-cooperation movement of 1920 to 1922 was the first campaign Gandhi led across all India. It turned the Indian National Congress from a club of lawyers into a mass movement.
